title: Inside the method
intro: Passing an array to a method passes a copy of the arrow, not a copy of the boxes. Predict what the caller's array holds once each method has run.

rounds.right: `arr` and `{name}` are two arrows to one array, so the caller sees the change: `{name}` is now `{result}`.
rounds.why: `arr` holds a copy of the arrow in `{name}`, so both point at the same array. `arr[i] = arr[i] + 1` writes into those boxes, and `{name}` sees every change.

rounds.right: `{name}` is still `{result}`. The squares went into a new array, which came back as the return value and now sits in `sq`.
rounds.why: `squares` writes only into `result`, a new array made with `new int[arr.length]`. It reads `arr`'s boxes but never writes to them, so `{name}` is untouched.

rounds.right: Even one write through `arr` changes the caller's array: `{name}` is now `{result}`.
rounds.why: One assignment through the parameter is enough: `arr[0] = 0` writes into the box that `{name}[0]` names too, because `arr` and `{name}` point at the same array.

rounds.prompt: The twist: this method points its parameter somewhere new. What does `{name}` hold after the call?
rounds.right: Moving the parameter's arrow never moves the caller's: `{name}` is still `{result}`, and the new array is thrown away when the method ends.
rounds.why: `arr = new int[arr.length]` points the parameter at a brand-new array, so `arr[0] = 99` writes into that one. `{name}` still points at the original.
